summary: Replace the plain k×k grid with a search over integer-grid packings: a skyline DP on an m×m grid (m up to 8, time-guarded) allows mixed square sizes with at most n squares. It is combined with a cheap block-merge family for larger m. The best candidate by total side length is returned, padded with z

Replace the plain grid with a recursive DP over k×k grids. Each grid may hold aligned b×b blocks, and every block or cell recursively holds its own optimal packing. The distribution of squares among items is found by a max-plus knapsack. This reproduces the known values for n=6, 7, 12 and 13 and gen

Cache the knapsack back-pointer table for each m when the DP picks a grid choice, so the build step reuses it instead of recomputing it. This is a speed and robustness change for larger n: it cuts the build-time cost and leaves the 40s DP guard in place.
Raise the maximum grid size in the recursive DP from 10 to 12 for m ≤ 150, so larger n have more grid and block options. The existing 40s guard stays, and the m > 150 path is unchanged.

Reduce the safety shrink on each square from 1e-12 to 2e-14 relative, so the sum of sides is almost exactly the DP value. Squares still do not overlap, since coordinate rounding errors are about 1e-16.

I added a second grid family to the DP: a k×k grid with two block sizes b1 > b2, placed first-fit, where every block and cell is packed recursively by the same knapsack. Add a greedy post-processing pass that grows each square into free space, anchored at each of its four corners. Where the DP leaves gaps, the sum of sides can only go up. Squares are never shrunk, and the growth is checked against every other square, so the packing stays valid.

Raise the maximum grid size in the recursive DP to 14 for m ≤ 60, where the knapsack is cheap, and keep 10 for larger m so the 40s guard still protects big n. This gives small and medium n more grid and block options.

I raise the maximum grid size to 12 for m ≤ 40, where the knapsack is cheap, and keep 10 for larger m so the 40s guard still protects big n. I also reduce the per-square safety shrink from 1e-12 to 1e-13 relative. I have not run it.
I reduce the per-square safety shrink from 1e-12 to 1e-13 relative, so the sum of sides is almost exactly the DP value. The packing logic is unchanged and I have not run it.

I made the knapsack table incremental, so each m only computes its own column instead of rebuilding the whole table. That cuts the DP from roughly O(J·m²) to O(J·m) per m. With the saved time I raise the maximum grid size to 12 for every m. I have not run it.

I raise the maximum grid size in the recursive DP from 10 to 11 for m ≤ 100, keeping 10 beyond that so the 40s guard still protects large n. I also reduce the per-square safety shrink to 1e-13 relative. I have not run it.

I cut the per-square safety shrink from 1e-12 to 1e-14 relative, so the sum of sides is essentially the exact DP value. Coordinate rounding is about 1e-16, so squares should still not overlap. Nothing else changes, and I have not run it.

I raise the maximum grid size to 12 for m ≤ 30, where the knapsack is cheap, and keep 10 for larger m so the 40s guard still protects big n. I also cut the per-square safety shrink to 1e-14 relative. I have not run it.

I raise the maximum grid size to 11 for m ≤ 60 (10 beyond that, so the 40s guard still protects large n) and cut the per-square safety shrink to 1e-14 relative. This gives mid-range n more grid options and keeps the sum of sides almost exactly equal to the DP value. I have not run it.

I added a "mixed" grid option to the recursive DP: one large b1×b1 block at a corner plus c2 blocks of size b2 anchored to the opposite corner, with the remaining cells packed recursively.
